title: Broad drain signal velocity leak caused multi-region misrouting and fallback surge - postmortem
creator: Anya Patel
incident_summary: A change to the region drain propagation heuristics introduced an overly permissive velocity window that allowed transient node-reports to be treated as global drains. This triggered multi-region route flushes, causing a surge of fallback model variants and elevated error rates for 18 minutes across eu-west-1 and us-east-1 traffic.
timeline: 2025-02-10T09:03:12Z - Synthetic load spike in eu-west-1 hit a set of GC events on a small percentage of nodes.
2025-02-10T09:03:30Z - New drain heuristic (merged earlier that week) evaluated a 3-sample velocity window and flagged local nodes as draining.
2025-02-10T09:03:35Z - Drain controller broadcasted node drain state without region-scoped dampening; routing plane initiated cross-region drains.
2025-02-10T09:04:05Z - Smart router began re-routing requests to fallback model variants; latency and errors started increasing on customer dashboards.
2025-02-10T09:20:00Z - On-call alerted by latency SLO alert and spike in fallback-rate metric; incident declared.
2025-02-10T09:23:40Z - Emergency rollback of the drain propagation change deployed (reverted commit), routing behavior began to normalize.
2025-02-10T09:28:00Z - Traffic and error rates returned to baseline; post-incident monitoring kept for 2 hours.
2025-02-10T11:45:00Z - Incident conference and initial triage notes captured on Confluence.
root_cause: A logic change intended to make drain detection faster reduced the region scope used to dampen drain propagation and used a short velocity window (3 samples) without requiring corroboration from the region leader. This allowed brief, local node events to be treated as authoritative and broadcast globally.
contributing_factors: Insufficient integration test coverage for multi-region drain propagation semantics.
The velocity heuristic parameterization was not clearly documented and lacked a safety gate in the rollout (feature flag enabled globally by default).
Alerting focused on node-level drains but not on cross-region drain amplification patterns.
Canary rollout was limited to a single cluster and did not exercise inter-region routing behavior.
immediate_actions: Reverted the commit that changed drain propagation (PR #12286).
Scoped the feature flag to a single non-production account and disabled global rollout.
Added temporary suppressor on the routing control plane to ignore drain reports that don't include region-leader confirmation.
Notified customers in the incident channel with a summary and mitigation steps.
long_term_remediations: Introduce region-scoped dampening: require leader corroboration or majority of local nodes before broadcasting drains across regions.
Add a circuit-breaker in the router to cap fallback amplification rate per region (tokens/sec limit).
Expand integration test harness to include synthetic inter-region GC/drain scenarios and assert no global broadcast on transient local events.
Implement progressive rollout policy for control-plane flags (percentage + region-aware rollouts).
Create a routing-simulator tool to model drain propagation and fallback amplification under adversarial node churn.
metrics_observed: Fallback rate: increased from 0.8% to 21% during incident window.
P95 latency: increased from 120ms to 520ms for affected endpoints.
Error rate (5xx): peaked at 3.6% from baseline 0.1%.
Cross-region drain broadcasts: 1 -> 14 within 45s indicating amplification.
links: slack:#incidents - incident channel thread (message permalink redacted)
lessons_learned: Rapid heuristic tuning without region-aware safeties can produce amplification failure modes in distributed control planes.
Feature flags must default to conservative scope; global-on merges for control-plane changes are high-risk.
Test coverage should include adversarial transient conditions (GC/IO spikes) that are common in production.
